THOUGHT: The lesion is a congenital/early-childhood, slow-growing, hypertrichotic, multinodular plaque on the trunk that has grown with the child — clinically this pattern strongly suggests a congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) or a neurogenic plaque such as a plexiform neurofibroma. Pathology is the decisive clue: the biopsy describes spindle/fusiform and dendritic cells with glassy eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent periadnexal (encircling terminal folliculosebaceous units) dermal involvement — histologic features classically seen in congenital melanocytic nevi (nevomelanocytes extend around adnexal structures). Immunoprofile shows diffuse S100 and SOX10 positivity with partial Melan A expression, which supports melanocytic lineage (Melan A is often variably expressed in congenital nevi, especially neurotized components). CD34 can be present in stromal fibroblasts/dendritic cells and does not exclude a nevus. By contrast, plexiform neurofibroma (an important clinical mimic given hypertrichosis, plaque morphology, MRI branching enhancement, and the patient’s focal café-au-lait macule, macrocephaly, and learning delay) would more typically show spindle cells with wavy nuclei in a myxoid background and usually lacks Melan A expression (S100 in neurofibroma is often patchy). MRI showing cutaneous lesion with branches into paraspinous soft tissues could represent deep extension of a CMN along dermal/subcutaneous structures or, less likely, a neurogenic plexiform lesion. Taken together, the most likely diagnosis is a congenital melanocytic nevus with deep/adnexal (neurotized) differentiation. Other top differentials include plexiform neurofibroma (NF1), deep-penetrating (neurotized) nevus or cellular/cellular blue nevus variant, plexiform schwannoma, and (less likely) a spindle cell melanoma/atypical melanocytic proliferation.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Congenital melanocytic nevus (neurotized / deep-penetrating/ adnexal-extending CMN) — best fits clinical hypertrichotic plaque, growth with the child, periadnexal invasion on histology, S100+/SOX10+/partial Melan A.
2. Plexiform neurofibroma (neurofibromatosis type 1–associated) — clinically plausible (plaque, hypertrichosis, MRI branching), S100+/CD34+, patient has some NF1-compatible features, but Melan A positivity and classic periadnexal nevus histology argue against it as the top diagnosis.
3. Deep-penetrating nevus / cellular (neurotized) blue nevus variant — can show spindle/dendritic melanocytes in mid–deep dermis with S100/SOX10 and variable Melan A, and present as a nodular plaque.
4. Plexiform schwannoma — S100+/SOX10+ multinodular tumor that can produce a plaque-like lesion; less likely given age, partial Melan A, and periadnexal nevus-like histology.
5. Spindle cell (congenital) melanoma or atypical melanocytic proliferation — very rare in this age group but considered because of deep dermal spindle melanocytes and partial Melan A; would require correlation with mitotic activity/atypia and possibly molecular testing to exclude.

Case Information:
A 17-month-old boy presented with a slow-growing, nontender plaque on the lower back. The plaque was initially 1 × 1 cm and had grown with the child. Medical history included dermal melanocytosis of the right hip and mid back, increased head circumference (97th percentile), and expressive language delay. No family history of congenital birthmarks.

Physical Examination:
Well-appearing boy with normal vital signs and Fitzpatrick type III skin type. On the left lower back, there was a 15 × 5-cm indurated skin-colored to yellow, firm, multinodular plaque with hypertrichosis, extending from the midline to the left lower flank. Additional blue-gray patches were present on the back and right hip, as well as a small café au lait macule on the right lower back. Limited neurologic examination was within normal limits.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Biopsy findings:    - Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed diffuse dermal infiltration of spindle cells, predominantly encircling terminal folliculosebaceous units    - Higher-power magnification revealed mix of partially fusiform melanocytes and dendritic cells with glassy, eosinophilic cytoplasm    - Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse and periadnexal S100 positivity in the mid to deep dermis    - Additional staining: Positive for CD34, SOX-10; Negative for desmin, SMA, CD1a; Partial expression of Melan A and epithelial membrane antigen  - Imaging:    - MRI of lumbar spine showed contrast-enhancing cutaneous lesion extending between L3-L5 spinal segment    - Branches of enhancement extending into paraspinous soft tissues of L4 and deep subcutaneous tissues of L3 spinous process    - No evidence of spinal involvement or dysraphism  Images included:  Figure A: Large, well-defined, firm yellow to skin-colored multinodular hypertrichotic plaque on the left lower back  Figure B: Hematoxylin-eosin staining of dermal infiltration (×4 magnification)  Figure C: Higher-power magnification of melanocytes and dendritic cells (×40 magnification)  Figure D: Immunohistochemical S100 staining (×4 magnification)
